overview: A four-page consular despatch from American Consul Gerald Warner in Taihoku to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on a sharp, delayed increase in the 1936 taxes assessed against the Taiwan branch of the Anglo-American Direct Tea Trading Company. Following representations by company manager R. Coughlin, Warner, acting manager D. Knight, and consular interpreter Matsuo met with the Taihoku tax authorities and learned that the company’s long-standing classification as a commission merchant had been replaced by taxation based on sales or consignments under new national, prefectural, municipal, and city-planning regulations. Although the company objected to the lack of notice and delay in billing, it accepted the new basis of assessment and agreed to cooperate more fully with officials.

subfiles.title: Despatch from Warner on increased taxation of an American tea company in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the reasons for, and consular discussions concerning, a threefold increase in the taxes levied on the Taiwan branch of the Anglo-American Direct Tea Trading Company.
subfiles.summary: R. Coughlin asked the consulate to investigate why the company’s 1936 tax bill, normally about ¥700–800 and paid in December, was delayed until September 1937 and increased to more than ¥2,500. Warner, D. Knight, and interpreter Matsuo learned that a tax expert from Tokyo had determined that the firm was incorrectly classified as a commission merchant and that new national, prefectural, city, and city-planning taxes were being assessed on its sales or consignments. Tax officials attributed part of the delay to inadequate access to the company’s books, while the company objected chiefly to the absence of warning and the late presentation of the bill. Both sides agreed to improve cooperation, and Knight accepted continued taxation on a sales basis, acknowledging that the firm had previously enjoyed favorable rates despite conducting more than ¥1,000,000 in consignment business during 1936.

interest: The despatch offers a detailed case study of how Japanese colonial tax administration in Taiwan affected a foreign trading firm on the eve of the Second Sino-Japanese War. It is especially useful for its reconstruction of the company’s privileged tax arrangement dating from 1927, the scale of its consignment trade, and the introduction of several layers of taxation in 1937. The exchange also reveals the practical limits of consular intervention: the consul helped secure an explanation and improved procedures, but neither challenged nor reversed the new assessment.
